_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 155 - Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855), ch. 13 'Hatupatu and his Brothers' (pp. 182-201). Topics 3 heroic tales, 9 sacred landscape, 4 founding. All passages are labeled paraphrase.

title.en: Hatupatu Killed by His Brothers and Revived
title.zh: 被兄長所殺的哈圖帕圖

region.en: Bird-snaring camps between Rotorua and Taupo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 羅托魯瓦至陶波之間的獵鳥營地（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 13, Hatupatu and his Brothers (London 1855)

summary.en: Snaring birds in the hill country, Ha-nui, Ha-roa and Karika give their little brother Hatupatu only lean tough birds; he eats and weeps together. He gorges himself on the stored calabashes of preserved birds, fakes a war-party raid - trampled paths, self-inflicted spear-wounds - and is exposed at last, killed by his brothers and buried in the heap of plucked feathers. His parents send the spirit Tamumu-ki-te-rangi, 'He-that-buzzes-in-the-skies', shaped like a flag, who performs enchantments over the grave and brings Hatupatu to life again.
summary.zh: 哈努伊、哈羅亞、卡里卡三兄弟入山獵鳥，只把瘦硬的鳥分給幼弟哈圖帕圖；他含淚進食。他偷吃光窖中整罐整罐的油漬鳥肉，偽造敵襲現場——踩亂小路、自傷數處——終被識破；兄長將他殺死，埋進拔下鳥羽堆成的大堆。父母派形似旗幟的精靈『天際嗡嗡者』塔穆穆基特朗吉尋屍施咒，哈圖帕圖死而復生。

sensitivity.note: Resurrection cluster: revival through a dispatched familiar spirit; interpretive tagging.

passages.text: Ha-nui, Ha-roa, and Hatupatu went to Whakamaru, to Maroa, to Tuata, to Tutuka, to Tuaropaki, to Hauhungaroa, to Hurakia, and to Horohoro - the districts which lie between Lakes Taupo and Rotorua and between Rotorua and the head of the Waikato River - to snare birds, and followed their sport for many a day. But their little brother Hatupatu was all this time thinking that they never gave him any of the rare dainties, but at each meal he received nothing but the lean tough birds; so when the poor little fellow sat down by the fire to his food he kept on crying and eating, crying and eating, during his meals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, whilst his brothers were out snaring birds and he was left to take care of the resting-place, the little rogue crept into the storehouse where the birds preserved in their own fat were kept in calabashes, and stole some and set resolutely to work to eat them with nicely beaten fern-root for a relish; so that to look at him you could not help thinking of the proverb, 'Bravo, that throat of yours can swallow anything.' He finished all the calabashes of preserved birds, attacked those kept in casks, then crept out and trampled over the pathway in all directions that his brothers might think a war party had come and eaten the food in their absence; then he ran a spear into himself in two or three places where he could not do himself much harm, gave himself a good bruise or two on the head, and lay down near the hut.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When his brothers came back they found him lying there in appearance very badly wounded, and the preserved birds all gone; he said a war party had done it, and they saw the footmarks and believed it. They melted fat and poured warm oil on his wounds, and he revived. Next day he stole again, every day, until at last his brothers laid in wait for him: 'Ha, ha, we've caught you now; your thievish tricks are found out, you little rogue?' His brothers killed him at once and buried him in the large heap of feathers pulled out from the snared birds. When they returned to Rotorua their parents insisted they must have killed him, for he went away with them and was missing on their return. At length Hatupatu's father and mother sent a spirit to search for him; its form was that of a flag, and its name was Tamumu-ki-te-rangi, He-that-buzzes-in-the-skies. It arrived at the place where Hatupatu was buried, found him, performed enchantments, and Hatupatu came to life again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.

title.zh: 哈圖帕圖與鳥女庫蘭蓋圖庫

region.zh: 紐西蘭羅托魯瓦瓦卡雷瓦雷瓦硫磺泉

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 13, Hatupatu and his Brothers (London 1855)

summary.en: Revived, Hatupatu meets a woman spearing birds with her lips; she has wings on her arms and carries him to her cave, where she eats only raw food. When he tricks her into hunting a thousand mountain ranges away, he roasts birds, kills her tame lizards and pets, and escapes with her cloaks and carved sword. Guided by the one surviving bird, Kurangaituku strides home in three steps, calling 'There you are, O Hatupatu, not far from me'; the fleeing youth charms rocks open and shut behind him until, leaping the boiling sulphur springs of Whakarewarewa, he watches her wade in and sink through the crust, burnt to death.
summary.zh: 復活的哈圖帕圖遭遇以唇為矛、臂生雙翼的鳥女庫蘭蓋圖庫，被帶回石穴；她食生冷，他假意進食。他誆她遠赴千山之外獵鳥，趁機烤鳥飽食，殺其馴蜥寵鳥，攜紅羽披風、狗皮斗篷與雕柄寶劍而逃。唯一的倖存小鳥飛報主人；鳥女三步即回，一路喊著『哈圖帕圖，你就在前面不遠』追趕。他念咒令岩石開合相阻，直到跳過瓦卡雷瓦雷瓦滾燙的硫磺泉；鳥女誤以為泉水冰冷涉水而過，陷入泉底被活活燙死。

sensitivity.note: Sacred-landscape record: explains the boiling springs and place-names of the Rotorua geothermal field; bird-woman as ogre.

passages.text: Hatupatu came to life again, and went upon his way, and met a woman who was spearing birds for herself, and her spear was nothing but her own lips: Hatupatu had a real wooden spear. The woman speared at a bird with her lips, but Hatupatu at the same moment threw his spear at the same bird, and it stuck into her lips; when he saw this he ran off with all his speed, but he was soon caught by the woman, not being able to go so fast as she could, for her feet bore her along, and wings were upon her arms like those of a bird, and she brought him to her house, and they slept there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hatupatu found that this woman never ate anything but raw food, and she gave him birds to eat without their being dressed; but he only pretended to eat them, lifting them to his mouth and letting them fall slyly. He remained at home while she went out spearing, cooking food for himself and looking at all the things in the cave of rocks she lived in - her two-handed wooden sword, her beautiful cloak of red feathers torn from under the wing of the kaka, her red cloak of thick dog's fur, her ornamented cloak of flax, her tame lizards and tame little birds - and he kept thinking how he could run off with them all. At last one day he told her to go a long distance to-day: to the first mountain range, to the second, the tenth, the hundredth, the thousandth range, and there begin to catch birds for them two. She consented and went; he remained roasting birds for himself, gathered up her cloaks and carved sword, brandished it and cut at the lizards and tame animals, killing them, and killed the perch of pet birds - all but one, which flew away to fetch back the woman, Kurangaituku, singing as it went, 'Oh, Kurangaituku, our home is ruined, our things are all destroyed.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kurangaituku made haste to get home, and as she went along kept calling out, 'Step out, stretch along; step out, stretch along. There you are, O Hatupatu, not far from me. Step out, stretch along. There you are, O Hatupatu, not far from me now.' She only made three strides before she had reached her cave, and could see nothing in it; but the little bird still guided her on, crying, 'I'll catch you there now, Hatupatu' - and she almost caught him, and he thought, I'm done for now. So he repeated his charm: 'O rock, open for me, open.' Then the rock opened and he hid himself in it, and the woman could not find him. Thus they went on the whole way, until they came to Rotorua; and when they arrived at the sulphur-springs called Te Whaka-rewa-rewa, Hatupatu jumped over these; but Kurangaituku, thinking they were cold, tried to wade through, sunk through the crust, and was burnt to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Hatupatu's Grass-Clump Army Takes Raumati's Head
title.zh: 草人疑陣取勞馬蒂首級

region.en: Maketu pa, Bay of Plenty, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭豐盛灣馬凱圖寨堡

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 13, Hatupatu and his Brothers (London 1855)

summary.en: Denied a command because of his brothers' jealousy, Hatupatu ties creeping-plant roots into bundles, dresses them in cloaks, and marches at dawn against Raumati, who burned the ancestral canoe Arawa. The enemy dreads the 'multitude of chiefs' in superb feathered dresses; the brothers' three real divisions break and fly, the mock army charges, and Hatupatu fells the chief Karika, takes his head, and slips away with Raumati's. Returning to Rotorua he chants over a basket of heads, reveals the hidden head of Raumati, and his father promotes his last-born above his eldest sons.
summary.zh: 因兄弟妒忌而被剝奪兵權的哈圖帕圖，夜裡把蔓草根莖捆成束、裹上披風，裝扮成一支雄師。破曉出戰：敵人畏懼他那『眾酋雲集、羽飾華麗』的假軍團；兄長三個真實方陣卻接連潰敗，唯有草人大陣沉然不動。哈圖帕圖擊斃敵酋卡里卡，割其首級，又暗中取走燒毀祖先之舟阿拉瓦號的仇人勞馬蒂的首級。歸舟唱勝，父親岸上發問誰得勞馬蒂之頭——三兄皆稱有，父親長嘆；哈圖帕圖自筐中高舉其頭，舉族歡騰，幼子由此凌駕長兄之上。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection; revenge for the burning of Te Arawa closes the canoe-cycle feud.

passages.text: His three brothers sprang at him, three wooden swords levelled at Hatupatu to slay him; he held the blade of his sword pointed to the ground till the swords of his brothers almost touched him, then rapidly warded off the blows, and whirling round his wooden sword, two of the three were felled by the blade of it and one by a blow from the handle; they sprang up and rushed at him once more, and over they went again - it was enough, they gave in. Their father said, 'Oh my sons, I would that you were as strong in peace as you are in attacking one another; in seeking revenge for your ancestral canoe, Te Arawa, which was consumed in a fire by the chief Raumati. Long have you sought revenge upon him, but gained no advantage; perhaps you are only strong and bold when you attack your young brother, my last-born child.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Three hundred and forty warriors were told off for each of the divisions under the command of each of Hatupatu's three brothers, but no division was placed under his command. He said, 'Oh my brothers, I did not refuse to hearken to you when you asked me to come with you; I came as you requested, just as I went readily with you upon that occasion when you killed me; I pray you, let some of the warriors be placed under my command, let there be fifty of them.' But they said, 'Pooh, pooh; come now, be off home again. What can you do? The only thing you are fit to destroy is food.' He said no more, but left his brothers, and on the same night sought out a rough thicket, turned to and began to tie together in bundles the roots of creeping plants and bushes, and dressed them up with the cloaks he had with him; the war band of these figures looked just like a band of real warriors.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: The day had hardly dawned when the inhabitants sent off messengers that they should come and fight with them against the common enemy. All the warriors of the columns of Hatupatu's brothers were exhorting their men; when they had all ended, Hatupatu himself got up to encourage his mock party, and as he gracefully arose it was beautiful to see his plumes and ornaments fluttering in the breeze; he made speech after speech, each time changing his dress and the knots of his hair - now a cloak of red feathers, now a bordered flax cloak, now dog-skins with the long war-axe, now the whalebone mere - so that the enemy, seeing how numerous were the chiefs in his column and what clothes and weapons they had, dreaded his division much more than those of his brothers; yet it was only formed of clumps of grass dressed up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now the people drew out to the battle, and pressed nearer, sending volleys of manuka spears at the column of Ha-nui; it is broken, they fly, they fall back on the division of Ha-roa, are rallied, but only poke forward their heads; the enemy is on them again; they run in upon the third line, that of Karika, and all the divisions of Hatupatu's brothers are broken and flying in confusion - what did it matter whether they were many or few, they were all cowards. All this time the division of Hatupatu appears sitting quietly upon the ground; when the men in full retreat came running in upon it, Hatupatu rose up crying 'Turn on them again, turn on them again!' At last they saw him; then rushes forward Hatupatu from one party and a chief of the enemy, named also Karika, from the other. The chief aims a fierce blow with a short spear; Hatupatu parries it, strikes him down with his two-handed sword, and motionless as food hidden in a bag, draws forth his whalebone mere, cuts off Karika's head, and grasps it by the hair. It is enough - the enemy break, fall back, fly; then his brothers and their warriors turn again on the foes and slay many thousands of them. Whilst his brothers are slaying the enemy, he eagerly seeks for Raumati; he is found; Hatupatu catches him, his head is cut off, and concealed. They return to Rotorua; his brothers in the canoe chant songs of triumph, and their father inquires from the shore which of them has the head of Raumati; one holding up the head he had taken said 'I have', and another 'I have', until their father calls out, 'Alas, alas! Raumati has escaped.' Then Hatupatu stands up in the canoe, chants a prayer to the god of war over a basket heaped with heads, grasps the head of Raumati which he had kept hid under his cloak, and cries, 'There, there; I have the head of Raumati.' All rejoice; their father strips off his cloak, rushes into the lake, and repeats a thanksgiving to the gods. When he had ended this, he promoted in honour his last-born child and debased in rank his eldest sons. Thus at last was revenge obtained for the burning of the Arawa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.
